title: Live the book
hook: proud of explaining Chrysippus? better to live what he wrote, and keep your principles like laws (Enchiridion 49–50)

segments.voice: Yesterday: prokopē, progress, and the checklist that starts with what you stop doing. Your line was blame no one. When did you feel the urge to blame, and let it pass? Day three hundred eighty-four.

There's a kind of person you meet at the gym. They know everything about protein timing, muscle fibers, the right angle for every lift. They'll explain it to you at length. They rarely lift. Philosophy has the same person, and so do plenty of hobbies: the one who can explain the book better than anyone, and whose life looks nothing like it. In Epictetus' school, the books students were proud to explain were by Chrysippus. Section forty-nine takes aim at the explainers. Today: live the book.
screen: `THE GYM EXPERT WHO NEVER LIFTS.` → `THE BOOK EVERYONE EXPLAINED.` → `LIVE THE BOOK.`

segments.voice: First, the book. Chrysippus was the third head of the Stoic school, and the ancient biographers say he wrote more than seven hundred works. And Epictetus' own joke implies he was hard to read. So in Epictetus' day, a student who could explain Chrysippus felt rather proud. Second, the deflation. When someone boasts that he can explain Chrysippus, Epictetus says, tell yourself: if Chrysippus had written clearly, this man would have nothing to boast about. Then he walks through it. What do I want? To understand nature and follow it. I find out Chrysippus explains it. I can't follow him, so I find someone who can explain Chrysippus. So far, nothing to be proud of. Explaining is only the doorway. Third, the turn. When I've found the explainer, what's left is to put the teaching into practice. That alone, Epictetus says, is something to be proud of. If all I admire is the explaining, I'm a grammarian, not a philosopher, just explaining Chrysippus instead of Homer. And when someone asks me to read Chrysippus to them, I blush, because I can't show actions that match the words. Fourth, the next section turns it into a rule. Whatever principles you've taken on, keep them like laws, as if breaking them would be a kind of sacrilege. And whatever people say about you, pay no attention. That isn't yours. Here, it's a fair question. Not how much can I explain. Which one line am I actually living?
screen: `CHRYSIPPUS: BRILLIANT, AND HARD.` · `EXPLAINING IS ONLY THE DOORWAY.` · `I BLUSH WHEN MY ACTIONS DON'T MATCH.` · `KEEP YOUR PRINCIPLES LIKE LAWS.` · then, large: `LIVE THE BOOK.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think back over everything you've read or heard on this path, or in any book that mattered to you. Let one line rise up, the one that's stuck. Maybe it's the other handle. Maybe it's wait. Maybe it's something older. Say it to yourself once. Now picture one moment today where you could live it, not explain it. See yourself doing it, in plain clothes, in an ordinary room. The bell holds the time.
Chrysippus. The Stoic writer whose books were hard to explain; explaining him is only the doorway, what counts is actions that match the words. Today's word.
Your line: actions that match the words. Live one line you've read today. Pick it, do it once, and don't explain it to anyone. Day three hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism choose a single principle from their reading and try to act on it for a day, rather than reading or explaining more.

fork.setup: a fellow student asks you to read and explain Chrysippus to him. how does Epictetus say he feels?
options: proud to show what he knows.
he blushes, when he can't show actions that match the words.
fork.reveal: explaining is no achievement. what he'd be proud of is living it, and he blushes when his actions fall short.

original.note: Greek: explanation, interpretation. Enchiridion 49 uses the related verb.

trapdoor: what you thought: read more books.
what it means: explaining a teaching is only the doorway; the only thing worth pride is living it.
what a scholar hears: Chrysippus, hard to read; explaining him without living him makes you a grammarian of a new Homer.

notes: Enchiridion 49 paraphrased: pride in explaining Chrysippus; 'if Chrysippus had not written obscurely'; I want to understand nature and follow it; seek the interpreter; the only thing to be proud of is to use the precepts; otherwise a grammarian explaining Chrysippus instead of Homer; I blush when I cannot show acts like and harmonious with the words. Enchiridion 50: abide by principles as laws, as if impious to transgress; disregard what anyone says of you. Confirm.
Diogenes Laertius 7.180 reports 705 books by Chrysippus. Confirm.
Greek ἐξήγησις: Epictetus uses forms of ἐξηγέομαι in Ench. 49. Confirm.
'Four hundred days into this path' is approximate (day 384).
